findings.claim: The Act of Uniformity restored a revised version of the earlier prayer book. Under Mary I, Parliament had repealed the law that authorized the book.
findings.explanation: The 1559 Act identifies the statute that authorized the book under Edward VI as the law Parliament repealed under Mary I. It then restores the book with specified revisions.

evidence.quote: authorized by Act of Parliament holden in the fifth and sixth years of our said late sovereign lord King Edward VI, intituled: An Act for the uniformity of common prayer, and administration of the sacraments; the which was repealed and taken away by Act of Parliament in the [Page 459] first year of the reign of our late sovereign lady Queen Mary
evidence.origin: Parliament of England, Act of Uniformity, 1 Elizabeth c. 2

evidence.quote: with the alterations and additions therein added and appointed by this statute, shall stand and be, from and after the said feast of the Nativity of St. John Baptist, in full force and effect
evidence.origin: Parliament of England, Act of Uniformity, 1 Elizabeth c. 2

findings.claim: Ministers were required to use the Book of Common Prayer for public worship.
findings.explanation: The statute requires ministers to use the book’s forms of public worship.

evidence.quote: all their common and open prayer, in such order and form as is mentioned in the said book
evidence.origin: Parliament of England, Act of Uniformity, 1 Elizabeth c. 2

findings.claim: The Act prescribed imprisonment for ministers lawfully convicted of refusing to use the required prayers.
findings.explanation: Refusal was a statutory offence. After a lawful conviction the Act required imprisonment. On a first offence it prescribed six months under the general rule and a year for a minister without a benefice or other ecclesiastical promotion.

evidence.quote: refuse to use the said common prayers
evidence.origin: Parliament of England, Act of Uniformity, 1 Elizabeth c. 2

evidence.quote: and shall be thereof lawfully convicted, according to the laws of this realm
evidence.origin: Parliament of England, Act of Uniformity, 1 Elizabeth c. 2

evidence.quote: the person so convicted shall for the same offence suffer imprisonment by the space of six months
evidence.origin: Parliament of England, Act of Uniformity, 1 Elizabeth c. 2

evidence.quote: shall not be beneficed, nor have any spiritual promotion, that then the same person so offending and convicted shall for the first offence suffer imprisonment during one whole year
evidence.origin: Parliament of England, Act of Uniformity, 1 Elizabeth c. 2

evidence.quote: repair to our Castell of Fotheringhaye where the said queene of Scottes is in custodie and cause by your commaundement execution to be don uppon her person

findings.claim: Robert Beale, the Privy Council’s principal clerk, delivered a copy of Mary’s death warrant to the Earl of Kent with a covering letter from the Council ordering the execution.

Its description of the acquired documents identifies the copy as an enclosure in the Council’s covering letter directing Kent to proceed with the execution.

evidence.quote: Robert Beale, principal clerk to the Privy Council of the time, was responsible for bearing the warrant to the commissioners
evidence.origin: National Heritage Memorial Fund and Lambeth Palace Library, account of the execution warrant acquisition

evidence.quote: This copy, which includes Beale’s annotation, was delivered by him to Henry Grey, 6th Earl of Kent, one of the two commissioners tasked with organising the execution. It was accompanied by a covering letter to the Earl from the Privy Council
evidence.origin: National Heritage Memorial Fund and Lambeth Palace Library, account of the execution warrant acquisition

evidence.quote: It was an enclosure in the Privy Council letter to the Earl of Kent, ordering the enactment of the execution
evidence.origin: National Heritage Memorial Fund and Lambeth Palace Library, account of the execution warrant acquisition

findings.claim: Elizabeth later said she had given no instruction to carry out the warrant.
